status: Researched 2026-08-18, revised after cross-check, imported 2026-08-19. Rows marked verified:false must not drive a headline number without the unverified badge. FOUR of twelve rows carry verified:true — the research's own prose says six, but the flags in its JSON say four and the flags are what the model reads, so four is recorded here and the discrepancy is noted rather than reconciled by editing a flag. Likewise the research reports 27 sources against 28 citation entries: the vessel-opex B row cites one Investing.com document twice for two different figures, so 27 unique documents and 28 entries are both correct. IMPORTED WITH TWO EDITS, both structural and neither touching a researched number: (1) datasetVersion date-stamped to match the sibling convention where the file stem equals the version; (2) ids remapped to the model's own vocabulary — the brief asked for `vessel.capexUsdM` and `vessel.opexUsdMPerYear`, which do not exist, because the model splits every vessel field by side. Each archetype runs ONE hull class on BOTH sides differing only by the separately-verified green premium, so a class-level newbuild-price range is the `fleet-capital` / `vessel-opex` GROUP, not a per-side field. Every low/mode/high, uncertaintyBasis and source is verbatim from the research.

rows.uncertaintyBasis: London maritime arbitration customarily allows a margin of 0.5 knots on speed and 5% on fuel consumption where the warranty is qualified by 'about', which fixes the symmetric contractual tolerance; the upside is skewed because performance warranties apply only on good-weather days (Beaufort 4 / Douglas Sea State 3 or better) and therefore exclude heavy-weather passages and progressive hull fouling between dry-dockings, both of which raise realised annual consumption above the warranted figure.

sources.title: Speed and Performance claims
sources.figureUsed: 'London Arbitrators usually allow a margin of 0.5 Knots in ship's speed and 5% in Fuel Consumption, when the phrase "about" is inserted'; good weather defined as 'the weather does not exceed Beaufort Force 4 and Douglas Sea Scale 3'
sources.note: Taken as the symmetric contractual tolerance around a warranted good-weather figure. Not itself the annual-consumption uncertainty: the warranty envelope excludes heavy weather, which is why the distribution is skewed upward rather than centred on +/-5%.

sources.title: Vessel Performance Monitoring: Speed, Fuel Consumption and Efficiency Analysis
sources.figureUsed: 'The word "about" carries a defined tolerance, commonly +/-5%, or in one case an allowance of 0.5 knots'; good weather 'wind not exceeding Beaufort Force 4 (maximum 16 knots) and total combined sea and swell significant wave height within Douglas Sea State 3'
sources.note: Independent corroboration of the +/-5% figure from a second, more recent source. Cited for the tolerance only; this outlet is a vendor blog and its Drewry-derived opex figures elsewhere are not used (see the findings note).

sources.title: Ship Fuel Consumption
sources.figureUsed: 'an allowance of 0.5 knots is reasonable for a ship's speed'; 'a ship's speed and fuel consumption might decline marginally due to aging or usage'; performance warranties valid 'in good weather conditions'
sources.note: Supports the ageing/fouling drift that motivates the upward skew. The pivotal authority cited is The Al Bida (1987), Court of Appeal.

rows.uncertaintyBasis: Widened from the deep-sea range because a short-sea feeder spends a materially larger share of its annual energy in port, manoeuvring and pilotage - none of which falls inside the good-weather sea-passage envelope that the +/-5% charter-party tolerance describes. The widening is a judgement, not a measurement: no source quantifying the port-energy share of a 1,800 TEU feeder's annual consumption was found.

sources.title: Speed and Performance claims
sources.figureUsed: 'London Arbitrators usually allow a margin of 0.5 Knots in ship's speed and 5% in Fuel Consumption'
sources.note: Same base tolerance as the deep-sea row. The widening to +0.18 is our judgement about the share of energy falling outside the warranted sea passage on a high-frequency short-sea rotation, and is not sourced.

rows.uncertaintyBasis: No price assessment exists for green or e-methanol: Ship & Bunker/MMSA publish methanol bunker indications for Singapore, Rotterdam, Houston and Fujairah, but for conventional methanol only. The range is built from the one signed RFNBO offtake (ACME-Mitsubishi Gas Chemical, USD 1bn for 100,000 t/yr over ten years = USD 1,000/t) bracketed by grey-methanol assessments plus the reported 2025 green premium of USD 200-400/t at the low end, and by e-methanol's documented exposure to renewable power cost at the high end.
rows.importNote: SCOPED TO C ON IMPORT. The research priced e-METHANOL; archetypes A and B run e-ammonia, whose band is already in the corridor bundle and already verified (640/900/1330 USD/t, Platts assessments + H2Global auction clearing). Applying a methanol range to those two would overwrite better data with worse. MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: this range currently reaches NOTHING. Only archetype B purchases its fuel (A and C build a plant, so their resolved merchant price is 0 and there is nothing to perturb), and B runs e-ammonia. The range is correct and it is inert here — it becomes live the moment a purchase-sourced methanol corridor is modelled, which is precisely the case a user is most likely to build. Kept rather than dropped for that reason, and recorded rather than left to look like an oversight.

sources.title: Methanol Price Trend 2026
sources.figureUsed: 'ACME Green Molecules finalises a $1 billion long-term deal to export 100,000 tonnes per year of green methanol to Japan's Mitsubishi Gas Chemical'; US methanol '~USD 592.74/MT in April and ~USD 586.35/MT in May'; China 'RMB 3.32/kg in April and RMB 3.16/kg in May'
sources.note: Our arithmetic: USD 1bn / (100,000 t/yr x 10 yr) = USD 1,000/t. Contract basis (delivered, FOB or ex-works) is NOT stated in any report of this deal, which is the single largest weakness in this row. Grey methanol figures are contract/spot assessments, not bunker-delivered.

sources.title: Methanol Market Size & Industry Share Report 2031
sources.figureUsed: 'Green-methanol premiums of USD 200-400 per ton in 2025'; 'Limited refueling capacity at only 15 ports worldwide'
sources.note: Our derivation of the low end: US grey at USD 586/MT plus the bottom of the premium band (USD 264) gives about USD 850/t. This is bio-methanol territory; the premium band is not disaggregated between bio- and e-methanol, which is why the row is verified:false.

sources.title: Green Methanol for Shipping 2026: Maersk's Bet & Supply Chain Challenges
sources.figureUsed: 'renewable power at 30-70 USD/MWh for e-methanol'; 'A change from 30 to 60 USD/MWh can easily shift fuel costs by several hundred USD per tonne'; premia of '70-150 USD per tonne of CO2 abated for the best bio-methanol routes and well above 200 USD/tCO2 for early e-methanol'
sources.note: Basis for the high end: the stated power-cost sensitivity of several hundred USD/t on top of the USD 1,000/t contract point supports about USD 1,450. This publisher states its figures are a synthesis of internal models and disclosed offtakes, with no external citation for the modelled values - the same weakness that flagged the model's existing band.

sources.title: Ship & Bunker, MMSA Begin Publication of Methanol Bunker Price Indications
sources.figureUsed: 'methanol bunker price indications for the four major bunkering hubs of Singapore, Rotterdam, Houston, and Fujairah', indicated 'in terms of energy equivalent pricing for both traditional VLSFO (MEoH-VLSFOe), and MGO (MEoH-MGOe)'
sources.note: Cited to establish what DOES exist and what does not: these are conventional methanol indications. No equivalent green or e-methanol assessment was found at any hub. The energy-equivalent convention (MEoH-VLSFOe) is worth adopting in the model's own reporting.

rows.unit: USD million per ship, conventional newbuild
rows.uncertaintyBasis: Five reported 2026 Supramax/Ultramax newbuilding contracts span USD 33.5m to USD 39.2m, with the spread driven almost entirely by build country: Chinese yards cluster at USD 33.5-35m and the one Japanese order (Nihon Shipyard/Imabari) sits at USD 39.2m, a 17% premium for the same deadweight.
rows.importNote: Researched as `vessel.capexUsdM` for the Handymax class. Imports as the fleet-capital GROUP: archetype A runs one hull on both sides, so a yard-price move lifts green and fossil together and their spread is the separately-verified green premium.

sources.title: Greek Shipowner W Marine Orders Three Ultramax Bulk Carriers at Dajin Heavy Industry
sources.figureUsed: 'The price of $33.5 million per vessel is slightly below recent market levels for similar Chinese newbuildings'
sources.note: Sets the low end. The source's own characterisation of the price as below market is why P10 is set at 32 rather than at this figure.

sources.title: Vessel order change: 4 conventional Ultramax and 6 Handysize newbuildings on shipbuilding menu
sources.figureUsed: 'four conventionally-fuelled 64,000 DWT Ultramax newbuilds for an aggregate consideration of $156.8 million ($39.2 million each)'; option on 'two 64,000 DWT dual-fuel (methanol/fuel oil) Ultramax newbuildings... for a total consideration of $91 million ($45.5 million each)'; 'All of these will be built by Imabari in Japan'
sources.note: Sets the high end for conventional. Note this order also prices the methanol dual-fuel premium at 45.5/39.2 = +16.1% from a single owner at a single yard - a cleaner like-for-like than most published premium figures, though the premium is out of scope here.

sources.title: Strong Newbuilding Ordering Still the Norm
sources.publisher: Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide (reporting Banchero Costa)
sources.figureUsed: 'Greek owner JME Navigation reportedly contracted 1x 64,000 dwt Ultramax at New Dayang Shipbuilding for approximately USD 35 million'
sources.note: Supports the mode. Broker-reported, so approximate by the source's own wording.

sources.title: Goldenport Orders Second Batch of Ultramax Bulk Carriers from Nantong Xiangyu
sources.figureUsed: 'two 63,500 DWT Ultramax bulk carriers... This second order follows a previous contract for two identical vessels signed in June at USD 35,000,000 per unit. The total program of four vessels is valued at approximately USD 140,000,000'
sources.note: Two independent orders at the same yard four months apart, both at USD 35m - the strongest single anchor for the mode. Note the model's row is a 58,000 dwt Supramax, smaller than these 63,500-64,000 dwt Ultramaxes, so the model's USD 34m point is reasonable for a Chinese-built vessel of that size.

rows.unit: USD million per ship, conventional newbuild
rows.uncertaintyBasis: Reported 2026 Newcastlemax and large Capesize contracts cluster USD 73.5-78.25m, with a 2024 assessed value of USD 69.63m for 180,000 dwt setting the floor of the recent cycle; the model's current USD 80.5m point sits above every conventional contract found.
rows.importNote: Researched as `vessel.capexUsdM` for the Newcastlemax class. Imports as the fleet-capital GROUP, per the note on the A row.

sources.title: Goldenport Orders Second Batch of Ultramax Bulk Carriers from Nantong Xiangyu
sources.figureUsed: 'five 210,000 DWT Newcastlemax bulk carriers for Cosco Shipping Development. These new vessels feature a methanol and ammonia-ready design, in an operation valued at USD 391,250,000'
sources.note: Our arithmetic: 391.25 / 5 = USD 78.25m each. Carries a methanol/ammonia-ready specification, which industry reporting indicates prices close to conventional, so this is treated as the top of the conventional band rather than a premium vessel.

sources.title: Strong Newbuilding Ordering Still the Norm
sources.publisher: Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide (reporting Banchero Costa)
sources.figureUsed: 'Cape Shipping S.A. is understood to have confirmed an order for 3x 181,000 dwt Capesize bulk carriers at Hengli Heavy Industry, priced at around USD 76 million each for delivery in late 2027'
sources.note: Sets the mode. A 181,000 dwt Capesize is smaller than a 210,000 dwt Newcastlemax, so this is if anything a conservative anchor for the larger class.

sources.title: Bulker newbuilding values at 15-year high: Values for newbuild vessels of 180,000 DWT up by c.5.45% from USD 66.09 mil to USD 69.63 mil
sources.figureUsed: 'Values for newbuild vessels of 180,000 DWT up by c.5.45% from USD 66.09 mil to USD 69.63 mil'
sources.note: 2024 vintage, used only to set the floor of the recent cycle. Described at the time as a 15-year high, which bounds how far below the 2026 contracts a P10 can defensibly sit.

rows.unit: USD million per ship, conventional newbuild
rows.uncertaintyBasis: One reported 2026 feeder programme prices three 1,800 TEU vessels at USD 93-99m in total, i.e. USD 31-33m each, and the source itself expresses the figure as a range rather than a contract price; the band is widened modestly at both ends because this is a single datapoint.
rows.importNote: Researched as `vessel.capexUsdM` for the 1,800 TEU feeder class. Imports as the fleet-capital GROUP, per the note on the A row.

sources.title: Goldenport lifts ultramax newbuild bet
sources.figureUsed: 'three 1,800 teu feeder containerships at China Merchants' revived Qingshan Shipyard this year, with deliveries running through 2027 and 2028. The feeder programme is estimated to be worth between $93m and $99m'
sources.note: Our arithmetic: 93/3 = USD 31.0m, 99/3 = USD 33.0m per vessel. The source says 'estimated', not contracted, and gives a range - so this row is verified:false on the strength of a single estimated programme value. A second independent feeder price would move it to verified.

sources.title: How Much Does a Container Ship Cost: Price by TEU, Newbuild and Secondhand in 2026
sources.figureUsed: 'A 1,000 TEU feeder leaving a Chinese yard today is a USD 20 million ship'; 'Newbuild figures are ex-yard prices for conventional propulsion'
sources.note: Order-of-magnitude corroboration only: linear interpolation from 1,000 TEU at USD 20m to 1,800 TEU would give about USD 36m, but newbuild price does not scale linearly with TEU, so this is used to bound the high end rather than to derive a value. Broker marketing content, not an assessment.

rows.unit: USD million per ship per year, excluding fuel
rows.uncertaintyBasis: Four listed dry bulk owners with similar average fleet deadweight disclosed daily operating expenses spanning USD 5,180 to USD 6,805 per vessel in Q2 2026 - a 31% cross-sectional spread between well-run public operators - to which a dry-dock accrual of roughly USD 450-800/day must be added, since the disclosed figures report dry docking separately.
rows.importNote: Researched as `vessel.opexUsdMPerYear` for the Supramax class. Imports as the vessel-opex GROUP for the same reason as fleet-capital: one hull class, both sides.

sources.title: Star Bulk Q2 2026 slides: earnings beat on cost edge, fleet scale
sources.locator: Q2 2026 results presentation, peer comparison slide
sources.figureUsed: 'average daily operating expenses (OPEX) of $5,180 per vessel in Q2 2026'; 'Star Bulk's daily OPEX of $5,180 compared favorably to peers ranging from $5,445 to $6,805, despite operating vessels with similar average deadweight tonnage'
sources.note: THE KEY SOURCE. A published cross-sectional spread across four listed operators explicitly normalised for average deadweight - the closest public equivalent to the fleet spread Drewry sells. Star Bulk's fleet is 138 vessels averaging 12.4 years, spanning Supramax to Newcastlemax.

sources.title: Star Bulk Carriers Corp. Reports Its Strongest Quarterly Results Since the Second Quarter of 2022
sources.figureUsed: 'Daily operating expenses per vessel, excluding pre-delivery expenses due to change of management and delivery of our newbuilding vessels, amounted to $5,180 for the second quarter of 2026 compared to $4,928 for the corresponding period of 2025'; 'Dry docking expenses for the second quarter of 2026 were $19.6 million'
sources.note: Confirms the disclosed figure EXCLUDES dry docking, which is reported as a separate line. The corridor model's OPEX field is specified to include a dry-dock accrual, so a per-day adder is required before comparison. Also confirms +5.1% year-on-year at this operator.

sources.title: Genco Q2 2026 earnings: Higher freight rates lift revenue and dividend
sources.figureUsed: 'Daily vessel operating expense increased 8.8% to $6,757 per vessel. Management attributed the increase to crew and insurance costs and the timing of purchases of stores and spare parts'
sources.note: Independent confirmation of the top of the peer band and, more usefully, a TIME-variation signal: +8.8% in a single year on crew and insurance. The band is set wider than the pure cross-section because of this.

sources.title: Star Bulk Carriers Corp. (SBLK) Stock Analysis & Key Metrics
sources.figureUsed: 'in the first quarter of 2024, SBLK reported daily opex of ~$4,972, which is significantly BELOW the ~$6,819 reported by its high-quality peer Genco Shipping (GNK) for the same period'
sources.note: Shows the same two-operator spread persisting two years earlier ($4,972 vs $6,819), so the 31% dispersion is structural rather than a one-quarter artefact. Secondary source; the underlying figures are from company filings.

rows.unit: USD million per ship per year, excluding fuel
rows.uncertaintyBasis: Same disclosed operator band as the Supramax row, shifted upward by a class premium of roughly 1.15-1.25x. Vessel operating cost scales far more weakly than deadweight because crew - about 42% of the total - is essentially flat between the classes (both carry some 20-22 seafarers, and minimum safe manning steps by gross tonnage are small). Only hull-and-machinery insurance (tracking a 2.2x hull value), lubricants (tracking engine power) and repairs scale materially, giving a weighted ratio near 1.24x against a deadweight ratio of 3.6x. No operator publishes opex split by class, so the premium is inferred from cost structure, not measured.
rows.importNote: Researched as `vessel.opexUsdMPerYear` for the Newcastlemax class. Imports as the vessel-opex GROUP, per the note on the A row.

sources.title: Star Bulk Q2 2026 slides: earnings beat on cost edge, fleet scale
sources.figureUsed: 'peers ranging from $5,445 to $6,805'; 'Newcastlemax and Capesize vessels, representing 44% of the fleet by vessel count'
sources.note: No operator publishes opex split by class, so the class premium is inferred rather than measured - hence verified:false. The inference is bounded: a blended average containing 44% Capesize/Newcastlemax cannot be far from the large-vessel figure.

sources.title: Star Bulk Q2 2026 slides: earnings beat on cost edge, fleet scale
sources.figureUsed: 'peers ranging from $5,445 to $6,805, despite operating vessels with similar average deadweight tonnage'
sources.note: The phrase 'similar average deadweight tonnage' is what makes this a SIZE-NORMALISED operator spread. It measures management efficiency, not class. Applying it to two different classes therefore requires an explicit class premium on top - which the first version of this row omitted, making the Supramax-to-Newcastlemax step only 1.09x. Corrected to 1.19x at the mode.

rows.unit: USD million per ship per year, excluding fuel
rows.uncertaintyBasis: No listed feeder container owner discloses technical operating cost separately: the largest pure feeder owner guides on USD 8,510 per vessel-day but that figure bundles voyage expenditure, G&A and ship management alongside OPEX, so it bounds the answer from above without giving it. The band is the dry bulk range widened at both ends.
rows.importNote: Researched as `vessel.opexUsdMPerYear` for the 1,800 TEU feeder class. Imports as the vessel-opex GROUP, per the note on the A row.

sources.title: MPC Container Ships Q1 2026 Earnings Call presentation
sources.locator: Forward Charter Backlog / projected EBITDA footnote, 27 May 2026
sources.figureUsed: 'Projected EBITDA based on Forward Charter Backlog reduced by operating costs of USD 8,510 per day and vessel (incl. voyage expenditures / OPEX / G&As / Shipman)'; fleet of 51 vessels, approximately 130,000 TEU
sources.note: An UPPER BOUND only. The USD 8,510 bundles voyage expenditure (fuel, port) and G&A, both of which the corridor model handles elsewhere; the pure technical opex is materially lower and is not disclosed. Fleet averages about 2,550 TEU against the model's 1,800 TEU row. MPCC's own 'Adj. OPEX per day' metric is defined in the same deck but its value is not in the public summary - obtaining it from the full financial report is the single cheapest way to move this row to verified.

rows.uncertaintyBasis: Published 2026 cost-of-capital work for OECD energy infrastructure gives real WACCs of 6.5-7.5% for unregulated electricity and gas transmission and 7.0-7.5% for utility-scale solar and onshore wind, which at a 2% inflation assumption is roughly 8.5-9.6% nominal; a 2026 US midstream energy assessment gives 9.8% nominal. The band is set below those figures at its lower end because shipping assets are mobile, liquid collateral that supports cheaper senior debt than fixed energy infrastructure.

sources.title: Discount Rates for Energy Infrastructure, prepared for AEMO for the 2026 ISP
sources.publisher: Oxford Economics Australia for the Australian Energy Market Operator
sources.figureUsed: 'regulated transmission and distribution assets for gas and electricity attract the lowest cost of capital at 3.0%'; 'Unregulated electricity transmission and distribution assets have a recommended WACC of 6.5%, slightly lower than 7.0% for unregulated gas transmission and distribution'; 'Utility-scale solar and onshore wind follows with a WACC estimate of 7.0% and 7.5% respectively'
sources.note: These are REAL WACCs - the report states the 3.0% lower bound is 'an inflation-adjusted simple average' of regulatory determinations. Our conversion to the model's nominal basis at 2% inflation gives roughly 8.5-9.6%. Directly relevant to scenario B (Australia).

sources.title: 2026 Capitalization Rate Study: Pipelines - Midstream MLPs
sources.figureUsed: 'WACC (Rounded) 9.80%'; capital structure 'Equity 58.00% / Debt 42.00%'; 'Selected Cost of Equity 13.19%'; 'Selected Cost of Debt 6.74%'
sources.note: Nominal, post-tax, for listed US midstream energy. A statutory valuation study rather than a project-finance quote, and midstream carries commodity exposure a contracted corridor would not - cited to bound the high end, not to set the central value.

rows.uncertaintyBasis: Utility-scale renewable project WACCs in a large emerging market run 8-10% nominal in 2026 having fallen from 14-15% in 2010 as offtake contracts standardised, with higher-risk project categories at 10-12%; the band is set slightly wider at both ends to span the range between a strongly-rated upper-middle-income sovereign such as Chile and a weaker one. INDIA IS A PROXY, NOT CHILE: Chile is a stronger sovereign credit and would plausibly finance nearer the OECD band, so this row should be replaced with Chile-specific project-finance evidence before it drives a published figure.

sources.title: WACC (Weighted Average Cost of Capital): Definition & Solar Finance
sources.figureUsed: 'Indian solar WACC in 2026 runs 8 to 10 percent for utility projects, 9 to 11 percent for C&I, and 10 to 12 percent for residential rooftop'; 'WACC has fallen from 14 to 15 percent in 2010 to 8 to 10 percent today as PPAs became standardised and projects more bankable'; 'Typical Indian solar leverage is 70/30 debt-to-equity'
sources.note: India is a proxy, not Chile. The research placed this caveat outside the sources array; on import it is folded into uncertaintyBasis so the caveat cannot be separated from the number it qualifies.

rows.uncertaintyBasis: Anchored on published central-bank target bands across the corridor set - 2% symmetric for the euro area and 2-3% for Australia - widened to reflect that a 15-year average smooths single-year shocks but that the 2021-23 episode demonstrates sustained overshoots are possible. No inflation-swap forward curve or historical dispersion study of 15-year realised averages was retrieved.

sources.title: Drewry: Ship operating costs reach inflection point as inflation returns
sources.figureUsed: 'overall vessel operating costs are expected to rise below the level of general price inflation over the next few years and so represent cost stagnation in real terms'
sources.note: Cited only to establish that shipping cost escalation is conventionally benchmarked against general price inflation rather than a sector-specific index - relevant because the model escalates operating costs at this single rate. This is NOT a source for the range itself, which is target-band judgement. Treat this row as the weakest in the file; its leverage (0.04-0.21) is also the lowest of the six items, so the cost of the weakness is small.
